children.text: The Patapat Viaduct is a concrete elevated road about 1.3 km long that runs along the coastal cliffs east of Pagudpud. With tropical forest on one side and the blue water of Pasaleng Bay on the other, it is the best scenic drive in northern Ilocos, and you can drive it and take photos for free.
The Patapat Viaduct is a concrete elevated road hanging beneath steep cliffs on the northernmost coast of Luzon, east of Pagudpud in Ilocos Norte. It is about
1.3 km
long and about
wide, carried on 76 spans roughly

above the sea, with forested Patapat mountainside on one side and the deep blue water of Pasaleng Bay on the other. It is an ordinary national road with no entrance fee and no gate, yet few roads in northern Ilocos are as dramatic.

The reason it exists is landslides, not scenery. Here the mountains drop straight into the sea, and every heavy rain used to bury the road under rocks and mud, so engineers chose to lift the whole road onto a structure along the shore beneath the slope. Built by Hanil Development Co., it opened to traffic in
October 1986

and has served ever since as the lifeline that links the Pan-Philippine Highway coming up from Manila to the Cagayan Valley. Its design life is reported as 45 years, so now that it is past 40, inspection and repair work is a constant part of its life.

For anyone driving it, the charm lies in the constantly changing views. The spans zigzag along the slope, so the balance of sea and cliff shifts at every bend, and on clear days the islands of Fuga and Calayan appear faintly on the horizon. Below, a pebble shore laced with white surf has become the first roadside viewpoint photographers look for.

If you only stop on the way to Pagudpud for photos, an hour is plenty, and it suits travelers touring northern Ilocos by rental car, motorbike or van. To reduce landslide closures, however, the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) has been building a second viaduct (Patapat Viaduct 2) on the same stretch since
October 2023
, and the road closes when it rains, so make a habit of checking road conditions before you set out. The total project budget is reported at about
; check the latest announcements for the completion date.

Heading east from Pagudpud town toward Cagayan, the sea opens up on your left; on the way back, the mountainside brushes past the right-hand window. The two directions feel like completely different roads, so ask your driver to go slowly.

The viaduct clings to the mountain and bends again and again, so from a distance its white railing runs along the cliff like a snake. Capturing the whole stretch in one frame from a roadside viewpoint is the most photographed composition.
Pasaleng Bay, which the viaduct overlooks, is a shallow bay about
16 km

east of Pagudpud town and a fishing ground for local fishermen. The water changes from emerald to deep navy with the weather, so you will find yourself pressing the shutter many times from the same spot.

blocks.title: Walk down to the pebble shore

children.text: A side path from the road leads down to a shore of rounded pebbles and rocks where you can look up at the piers from below. Waves can be dangerous on rough days, so do not stand too close to the water, and stay away from the slope side where rocks may fall.

On a clear day, look at the northern horizon and you may see the faint outlines of Fuga and Calayan islands in the Babuyan group. On low-cloud days in winter they are invisible, so treat them as a bonus that takes a little luck.

Early in the morning there is little traffic and the light is soft, so the road and railings photograph cleanly. At dusk the sky turns red and the mountain shadows deepen, changing the mood, and photo enthusiasts sometimes come in the late afternoon on purpose.

This is a small shrine and a spring flowing down from the mountain beside the main road just past the viaduct. Stories tell of a healer named Anton who cured the sick here. With no stairs to climb and no trekking needed, it is a pleasant stop to step out of the car, wash your hands and rest a moment. If there is a small donation box, it is polite to drop in what you can.
The viaduct runs through the middle of Kalbario–Patapat Natural Park, a protected area of about 3,800 hectares designated in

. Just seeing the dense tropical forest pour down to the sea from the road explains why this stretch is protected. Trekking inside the park may require a separate permit and a guide, so ask the tourism office.

Arrive in Laoag
Doing all of this in one day from Laoag means long driving and a rushed schedule. If you have time, we recommend staying one night in Pagudpud.
Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific fly nonstop from Manila to Laoag International Airport (LAO) in about
1 hour 10 minutes
, with one-way fares of about
. From the airport to the Patapat Viaduct it is about
, roughly
2 hours 30 minutes
by car. The easiest way is to get a rental car or a van with driver at the airport and drive up to Pagudpud.
Many night and day buses run from Manila terminals such as Sampaloc and Cubao to Laoag. The trip takes about
9–11 hours
, with fares of roughly
for regular,
for super deluxe and
for sleeper. Some direct services to Pagudpud exist, but they are infrequent, so most people change in Laoag.
From the Laoag north terminal, a bus toward Pagudpud or Cagayan takes about
2 hours
and costs about

. Buses toward Cagayan do pass over the viaduct, but there is reportedly no official stop, so people get off in Pagudpud town and take a tricycle, or ask the driver in advance to let them off by the roadside. Catching a ride back means flagging down a passing bus at an uncertain time, so we recommend having your tricycle wait for you.
From Laoag, follow the Pan-Philippine Highway (Maharlika Highway) north. It is about
72 km
to Pagudpud town, and the viaduct lies another
east. The road is in good condition, and the drive from Laoag takes about
2 to 2 hours 30 minutes
. A van with driver for a day costs about
From Pagudpud town to the viaduct is about
20–30 minutes
by tricycle. Drivers usually quote about

for a half-day tour combined with Kabigan Falls, Blue Lagoon and so on; if you ask only for a round trip to the viaduct with waiting time, you can bargain it lower. Many travelers also rent a motorbike and ride themselves, available from shops near the lodgings for about
a day.
You can drive the viaduct all year, but the clearest and safest time is
December–May
. Especially in
March–May
the sea is calm and the sky clear, so the color of Pasaleng Bay and the distant islands are sharpest. Daytime temperatures here hover around
all year, so the midday sun is strong; early morning or late afternoon is better.
From
December–February

the northeast monsoon brings high waves and low clouds on many days. The scenery looks moody, but white surf breaking under the piers is actually a highlight of this season. Even so, the national road through Pagudpud was blocked by major landslides in
December 2023
, so leave extra time if rain is forecast.
June–September
is the rainy season, when rainfall here is heaviest, and typhoons crossing northern Luzon are frequent from
July–October
. In heavy rain or a typhoon, falling rocks and landslides can close this stretch, so it is better to postpone. Annual rainfall in Pagudpud is reported at about 1,985 mm.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
There is no lodging around the viaduct itself, so visitors normally stay in Pagudpud town or around Saud Beach and Blue Lagoon. The Saud Beach area has many family resorts with rooms at about
a night, while homestays and guesthouses in town run about
. All of them are around
20–30 minutes
by car from the viaduct, so an early-morning visit is no trouble.

Small stalls selling coconuts and drinks appear now and then along the roadside, but for a proper meal you need to go back to town. Typical Ilocano dishes include pinakbet (vegetables sautéed and seasoned with fermented fish sauce, bagoong), crispy fried pork bagnet, and grilled fish and squid. A sour vinegar dipping sauce, popular among Ilocanos, whets the appetite. Before starting a northern tour, it helps to buy a packed lunch and water in town.
The viaduct is a working national road where vehicles speed past. When taking photos, always park on the shoulder or at a designated viewpoint, and never stand in the middle of the road.
A 15-ton load limit sign stands at the entrance to the viaduct. When a large bus or truck passes, step back from the railing.
The best photo times are early morning,
, and late afternoon,
. At midday the light is harsh and the sea washes out to white.
This is a protected area and a national road, so drone photography may need a permit. Check the rules with the tourism office before flying.
Phone signal is weak in places, so download an offline map beforehand.
Tell your tricycle or van driver in advance how long you want to stop for photos so you are not rushed.
The quickest way to learn road conditions is to ask the Ilocos Norte tourism office in the Laoag provincial capitol, or your lodging.
Bring sunglasses, a hat and a thin windbreaker. The sea wind is surprisingly strong, and your hat can blow away at the railing.
The stretches on either side of the viaduct are known as some of the Philippines' most landslide- and rockfall-prone. During rain, or right after it stops, do not stand close to the mountain slope.
Wet pebbles and rocks are very slippery when you go down to the shore. On high-wave days stay well back from the water, and do not swim.
A second viaduct is under construction right beside it, and a repair schedule for the existing viaduct was published for
February–August 2025
. Construction vehicles and slow-traffic sections are possible, so check the latest announcements.
Just beyond the railing is the rocky shore, so do not let children climb or lean out, and watch for traffic behind you when stopping on the shoulder.
After dark there is little light and many bends, and night driving here is said to be dangerous. Plan to be back in town before sunset.

On days when a typhoon approaches or a heavy-rain warning is issued, the national road through Pagudpud can be closed without warning and you may be stuck for hours. Always check the weather forecast and local government announcements before departing.
Pagudpud town and Saud Beach are about
20–30 minutes
west by car. With lodging, restaurants, swimming and surfing, it makes a good base for the viaduct.
